newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Three cosmonauts back on earth after Mir mission.
newsitem.headline: Three cosmonauts back on earth after Mir mission.

text.p: Three cosmonauts returned to earth on Sunday after conducting a range of scientific experiments aboard Russia's orbiting Mir space station.
"Everything went according to plan. The landing capsule (from the Soyuz TM-24 spacecraft) came down on schedule at 0944 (0644 GMT)," a mission control spokesman told Reuters.
The three cosmonauts, Russians Valery Korzun and Alexander Kaleri and Germany's Reinhold Ewald, landed at a remote location some 130 km (80 miles) east of the Kazakh town of Dzhezkasgan.
Itar-Tass news agency said the cosmonauts, "felt well" after their mission and would be flown later on Sunday to a location just outside Moscow for routine post-flight medical tests.
"I'm very glad to be going home," Ewald told mission control in televised comments shortly before leaving Mir.
Kaleri said, "it was great working here and I am disappointed to leave this home but now we have another home to go back to."

Ewald spent 20 days in Mir, carrying out medical and technical research. He flew under an agreement between Germany and Russia in which Bonn will pay millions of dollars for the ride -- a welcome fillip for Moscow's struggling space industry.
Germany has said it considers the Ewald flight important as preparation for a return to the international Alpha space station that is due to replace the ageing Mir in the future.

The two Russians blasted off from the Baikonur cosmodrome in Kazakhstan last August and conducted more than 200 experiments in new scientific modules aboard Mir under programmes sponsored by the United States, France and Russia.

Russians Vasily Tsibliyev and Alexander Lazutkin are scheduled to remain aboard Mir along with U.S. astronaut Jerry Linenger, who began to work at the station on January 15. They are scheduled to return to Earth in June.

Last Sunday all six cosmonauts were forced to don gas masks when fire broke out on the Mir station, the latest in a series of mishaps to bedevil the 12-year-old station, which is the world's only permanent orbiting craft.

It happened hours before Russian space officials announced money troubles had forced a delay in the launch of the first module of the Alpha station, casting new doubts over Moscow's ability to participate in the international project.
The Russian Space Agency said the first Alpha module would now be launched next year, rather than this November.
The new space station, to be completed by 2003, is being funded by Russia, the United States, the European Space Agency, Canada, Italy and Japan.
Russia is building the first module, a cargo section, and the third, a service area where cosmonauts will live and work.
Some U.S. officials already say Moscow, which also blames cash shortages for long delays in building the third module, is not pulling its weight.

A delay in launching the first module will also delay launch of the second stage, a docking module being built in the United States. After the third module, other parts of the station will be attached in stages by 2003.

The 120-tonne Mir space station was first launched in 1985, and is expected to be in use until 1999, when the Alpha station would become the world's primary vehicle for long-term space endurance. Mir has been manned continuously since 1989.
